beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: The judge stays fixed; that keeps the loop's score meaningful.
beats.got: Something called a judge scores the output and a generator improves while I'm away, but I don't know what a 'Module 5 eval' is yet.

beats.trigger: Start with the judge you saved at the close of Module 5.
beats.got: Read a Mollick piece and find my old judge file.

beats.trigger: **Build** a self-improving eval loop: separate agents generate and judge, the Module 5 judge scores each round unchanged
beats.got: I will build something technical. Nothing here says what it means for my people.

beats.trigger: Can agents improve if you define the outcome and let them find the path, or does organisational mess still matter too much?
beats.got: Mollick's question is about whether companies are too messy for agents to improve by themselves. That is a question I can take to the leadership team.

beats.trigger: the system absorbs the catches without you.
beats.got: The work improves without a person involved, and my first thought is who that person used to be.

beats.trigger: Humans will not cope with all the detail for long. You can stay inside one loop. You cannot stay inside all of them.
beats.got: People can't review everything, so what 'good' means has to be written down for the system. That is a management problem as much as a technical one.

beats.trigger: one briefing, thirty claims, four detectors, one scorer.
beats.got: A recap of Module 5's setup. I only half remember it, and 'detectors' was never explained to me.

beats.trigger: every claim cites evidence or admits the gap.
beats.got: Groundedness means everything in the output traces back to a source.

beats.trigger: Two mails both avoid overclaiming; one is forgettable, the other makes the reader act.
beats.got: Being correct isn't enough. You also need a check for whether the mail is useful. I would want this for HR communications.

beats.trigger: If the judge moved, the score means nothing.
beats.got: The rule of the loop: only the generator changes, never the judge. That's like not changing the marking criteria mid-exam.

beats.trigger: You decide which details the system must never miss.
beats.got: Choosing what the system must never miss is a human decision. I could ask my HR partners which details in people matters must never be missed.

beats.trigger: Run at least three rounds, then continue until improvement stops.
beats.got: A 45-minute exercise where I run a loop. 'Main session' and 'helper agents' are used before I know what they are.

beats.trigger: Note what the judge catches; the tactic must learn that.
beats.got: I ran the judge once by hand to see what it catches. It flagged a few claims in the briefing.

beats.trigger: While the loop runs, ask about parallel search:
beats.got: I started the loop and waited. The side prompts on parallel search and model training have nothing to do with my people questions.

beats.trigger: weak claims marked grounded mean the judge has a blind spot.
beats.got: I read the loop result. The SHA check shows the judge didn't change. I can follow it, but I'd have no idea whether the numbers are good.

beats.trigger: And you weren't there.
beats.got: The tactic got better each round while I was away. It's a bit eerie but also impressive.

beats.trigger: You do not inspect every output; you design the loop and own the yardstick.
beats.got: My job in this picture is to own the standard, not to check every item. That is a role I recognise from managing.

beats.trigger: Take-home: put any judge in a loop that improves the thing it scores.
beats.got: I could wrap the loop around another judge, but I haven't got one in mind yet.

beats.trigger: That does not mean the work is done.
beats.got: A score near zero doesn't mean the work is finished.

beats.trigger: A flat score is information about the judge, not the work.
beats.got: When the number stops moving, the judge has run out of things to see, and that's when human judgment has to come back in.

beats.trigger: A generator that grades itself passes itself.
beats.got: Nobody checks the judge unless I score a few outputs by hand and compare. A fair point, and it applies to people processes too.

beats.trigger: No release so far has told anyone what good means in your company.
beats.got: Better models will not define quality for us. We have to name it.

beats.trigger: The destination is not "the human disappears." You move one level up: you design the loop and own the yardstick.
beats.got: The module's answer to my headcount worry is that people move up a level. It's a claim, not yet evidence, but it's the first time the module spoke to me.

beats.trigger: What would have to be true before you let the agent hit send?

beats.got: A recap of floor and ceiling, now put as trust problem versus usefulness problem.

beats.trigger: Ask whether you have designed the loop that makes sending responsible.
beats.got: The question for me is whether the loop is designed to make sending responsible, and where a human is still needed. That is a question I can take to the leadership team.

beats.got: I made a steering check for internal mail. It could be something I show an HR partner.

beats.trigger: Every clean week is evidence the loop works, and each one erodes your ability to tell when the loop stops.
beats.got: The better the system works, the worse we get at noticing when it fails. That applies to people too.

beats.got: A summary list of model, context, tools, goal and so on. I understand the idea of earning autonomy, but it never says who in the organisation gets to design these loops.

beats.got: Ask the agent to sharpen the tactic file and push back where it's off. More tool work.

beats.got: A good tip: challenge the agent when its summary sounds too kind.

beats.trigger: You design the loop and own the yardstick.

take_homes: Correct is not the same as useful. I need one check that the output is grounded and another that it is good for the reader.
When the score goes flat, the judge has run out of things to see, not the work. Someone has to check the judge by hand against their own verdicts.
My job moves to deciding what 'good' means and when a human still has to read the output. That is a conversation to have with the leadership team.

monday.move: Take one HR communication an agent could draft, such as a role-change note or an onboarding mail, and write down in plain words what 'good' means and what must never be missed. Then show it to one HR business partner.
monday.who: Me, plus one HR business partner
monday.when: Monday, 30 minutes, before any tool is opened
monday.stop_condition: Stop if the HR partner can't tell from the written standard whether a mail passes.
monday.blocker: Employee data in an AI tool needs the works council and the DPO, and I haven't asked yet. I won't use real employee data until I have.

misconception.why: The module never discusses which roles go or stay. 'The human moves one level up' is reassuring, but it's asserted, not shown. I still expect headcount questions in the next leadership meeting, and now I have a better frame for answering them, not a different belief.

one_line: The middle part about floor versus ceiling, checking the judge, and where humans stay in the loop was worth my time. The exercise itself was a lot of technical steps with little said about people.
